utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today, we are Wednesday, the 4th of June, 2008. I'd like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom today. We have a witness who has been scheduled today, who has been granted protective measures. If there are no changes to the schedule, we shall drop the blinds, bring the witness into the courtroom, and I shall have a few questions to put to him before he takes the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I have a procedural issue, if you give me the floor. Do I have the floor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am surprised, first of all, by this partition here. Second, I'm surprised to hear you say that this witness enjoys protective measures, because I was served yesterday with a urgent motion by the Prosecution for protective measures for VS-55 -- 1055, dated 28th May, 2008, and the Prosecution gives the rationale for its motion. Maybe you have already made a ruling on this, but if you have, you did so improperly because you did not give me a chance to state my opinion. I have seven days to state my opinion. If you did not make a decision, then this witness does not enjoy protective measures. If he does not enjoy protective measures, then I insist that this partition be taken out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going rather too fast. We shall move into closed session, to begin with. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-1055, what was the ethnic composition of your village before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ethnic composition, as far as I understand, was around 45 per cent Serbs, 45 per cent Muslims, and some 10 per cent Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you describe the relationship between these different groups before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relations were good, extremely good. You could even say "excellent."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when things changed so that the relationship between the various groups became different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the developments throughout the country, tensions gradually were heightened, and the action taken by the municipality of Ilijas, which added tension, forcibly annexed the town of Ilijas and the whole municipality to the Serbian Autonomous District of Romanija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had -- what entity had Ilijas municipality been a part of before the events you just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality belonged to the city of Sarajevo, together with Vogosca, Ilidza, Trnovo, Pale, and Hadzici municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the Serbian Autonomous District of Romanija. Do you know when that was created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say precisely when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it created before the decision that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What parties were in the Municipal Assembly of Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Municipal Assembly of Ilijas, the Serbian Democratic Party was represented, the Party of Democratic Action, SDA, HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, and in a small percentage, reformist forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the leaders of these parties in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party -- the leader was Ratko Adzic. The Party of Democratic Action was led by Fehim Mesetovic. And the Croatian Democratic Union, Jozo Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember about at what -- sorry. Do you remember the approximate time that the decision was taken that Ilijas municipality should be part of SAO Romanija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was in March, the month of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you saw armed formations appearing in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see armed formations appearing in the town of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When about was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That started happening at the end of March and the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any of the leaders of these armed formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The leaders of these armed formations, or the leader, was Vasilije Vidovic, nicknamed Vaske.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that we move into private session again for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-1055, you described where Vaske had been before he reappeared in Ilijas municipality. Did you ever overhear any discussions where this was being talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know -- apart from what you've just described about how you know where Vaske had been before he came back to your municipality, have you ever overheard any conversations or anything like that which informed you about where he had been?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This is an improper question. "Did you perhaps ever overhear any conversations?" That's how it read. Now, what does that mean? A proper question would be, "Did you have any knowledge of," not, "Did you ever overhear any conversations?" I don't assume the witness is going to testify about what he overheard. That's hearsay. But the proper way to put the question is as I put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, rephrase your question. I personally found it difficult to understand the question, as all of this is rather confused, so put a broader question to emphasise what you wish to emphasise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-1055, apart from the book that you have mentioned, have you learned of where Vaske was from any other source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The office that I worked in was about 60 to 70 metres away from Vaske's flat, and on one occasion, from his flat, most probably without Vaske's knowledge, his father, Jovo, took out photographs from the battle front in Knin, and he boasted about the successes his son had had. He boasted to all the passersby, everybody that went past the shop I was working in. I did not go up to him to look at the photographs, but I assumed that those were the ones, Vaske's photographs from the front, from the battlefield, which his father confirmed to me orally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to us how the men -- how the group that Vaske had with him looked?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do we suddenly come to a group of people, "the group"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The witness testified that he saw armed formations in his municipality and that these armed formations were led -- and the leader of these armed formations were -- was Vaske. Okay, I can put the question without --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness can please describe how the armed formation that Vaske was the leader of looked, if the accused is opposed to the use of the word, "group."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My information to the effect that they were Vaske's soldiers is derived from the following. All those people were from the Knin battleground and they had come to a funeral of a friend of theirs who had been killed at Knin. His name was Margetic. I don't know his first name, but his surname was Margetic. They had come to attend the funeral and after the funeral, they all stayed on. The population complained about the presence of people in uniform in town, and then one day, over the local radio station, the mayor of the town, Ratko Adzic, informed the population that these people would be staying there for just a short while, that they were there to attend the funeral, and because Vaske had been wounded, and that they would leave and withdraw. But they never withdrew. They wore various uniforms, but all of them had a belt with knives stuck to the belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing any kind of insignia or -- well, were they wearing any kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had insignia belonging to the Chetnik organisation; that is to say, a skull, or a cockade, or the fur hat, or the sajkaca type of cap, all denoting that they belonged to that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd like if the Registrar would please call up 65 ter number 7222, and if we can go to page 79 of that exhibit. And, Your Honours, it is in your witness folder under tab 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I don't seem to have that tab. All I have is this [indicates]. I was given a binder to go with the previous witness, whereas I don't seem to have tab 3. I just have the exhibit numbers. So could the Prosecutor repeat the exhibit title, because I have no tabs here at all. It hasn't been tabbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us in which tab we can find this? There are two numbers which enable us to locate the document, and can you give us a page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me just consult the copy that we have of what Your Honours have been given. Sorry, maybe there are two questions. The page number in this document we need to look at is page 79. The title of the document is "Insignia and Uniforms Worn by Serbian Armed Forces during the 1991 to 1995 Conflict." The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. To help Mr. Seselj, this must be the document which -- well, you can see in red, on the left-hand side of the document, you can see the number "06323424."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I cannot open it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm informed that there's a problem opening the document, so maybe we can use the ELMO instead, if the usher will assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let the usher put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-1055, while we're waiting for these technical things to be sorted out: How many men were there with Vaske?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The document is now displayed in e-court, I think, so should we rather proceed with that or the ELMO? I'm at the disposal of the Registrar, really. We'll do the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1055, I'm going to show you a series of pictures, and I'd like you to tell me whether or not -- tell the Court whether or not any of the things that have been shown to you were seen by you at the time with Vaske's men. So, first of all, this is from page -- for the record, from page 79 of the exhibit. Did you see this insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This insignia was on the vehicle used by Vasilije Vidovic, Vaske.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can open the next page of this exhibit, page 80.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. You are asking him whether he has seen this. You must ask him where and when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1055, where was this insignia seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This insignia I saw on the caps and fur hats, the subara of the soldiers I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can go to the subsequent page, 81.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here we have another insignia. Is this one that you recognised from the time, and if so, when did you see it or where was it seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't notice what was written, but I did notice the emblem, not the words, on caps, on the uniforms, on the subaras or fur hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can move to page 82, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the same question: Is this an insignia that you saw at the time, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All this insignia belonged to those soldiers. Some of them had them as badges, others had them on their caps, yet others had them on their shoulders and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we move to page 91, please, of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1055, did you see something like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the fur hat, but I don't think I saw this insignia. Actually, I didn't have the courage to come up close to have a look, but I'm sure that that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here we have another hat. Did you see something like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that worn by anyone, and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This kind of cap was worn by Vasilije Vidovic, Vaske, in the attack against my village, and I'll come to that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And page 93, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this picture, does that resemble people that you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the people? Well, they were characteristically wearing this kind of clothing, that is to say, uniform, caps, beards, the insignia, as I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with this exhibit. I'll request -- or I'll ask that we have the document, or at least the pages that have been shown to the witness be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the pages shown to the witness will be Exhibit P455.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will prepare an extract with the relevant pages that we will upload into e-court so we have only the relevant pages as an exhibit under the list number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1055, did there come a time when roadblocks were set up in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the Serbian authorities, with the proclamation of SAO Romanija, took control of the police station, that's the time when the roadblocks were set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was already at the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was manning the roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The roadblocks were manned for a time by the locals, the locals of a particular place, because the Stavinja, Podlugovi, and Vratnica roadblocks were set up, in those places, so that the police station of Ilijas, which had been taken control of by the Serb -- the authorities of the Serb municipality of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe -- you mentioned that the Serbs took over the police station in Ilijas. Could you describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not near the police station, because I was going about my regular duties on that day. I was in the shop. But I heard that the police forces or, rather, the policemen came from other parts, like Zenica, Visoko. They'd already crossed over into Ilijas territory, and with the other Ilijas policemen they took control of the police station and set up their own people there in leading positions, as commander or the chief of the two services and all the other police services. The Muslims left their work posts together with the Croatian policemen, and an agreement of sorts was reached about the division -- or, rather, the handing out of weapons, whether it belonged to the Territorial Defence or the police force or whatever. But I do know that part of the weapons reached my place, and in charge was the commander of the then-police force, Omer Spahic. Omer Spahic returned to his native village. He hailed from, as we call it, the upper part, which is the Nisicka Plateau, and the person who remained with the weapons was -- well, called him up on the phone once - the telephone was still working. He said he didn't know what to do with the weapons because there weren't enough men, there was no reserve police force, so he didn't know what to do with the weapons. And that conversation, telephone conversation, was intercepted in the post office somewhere by the Serb policemen, and arrived immediately and took away those same weapons. And this action was led by a commander called Markovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when Markovic came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Markovic arrived with some of his men, and he demanded that the weapons be handed over. Well, he had heard that the weapons were there. And our people complied; they handed over the weapons just as they had received them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-1055, you have described these developments. Did you at some point in time see military equipment being deployed in Ilijas municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see military equipment brought into Ilijas. It had been brought sometime long ago. But we could see from our houses military vehicles moving through the hilly areas, more precisely through the local community of Ljubnici, which borders with Cekrcici towards Visoko, with only the Bosna River between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to discuss one more issue with respect to Vaske's group. Were any kind of privileges given to men from his group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men from his group were put up partly in his apartment and some in his house in Podlugovi for all their support, the wine and spirits. They needed food and the rest. It was the teacher of mathematics in Ilijas who was in charge of providing that. He ordered my colleagues to provide all the financial help and assistance in kind whenever their vehicles arrived to pick it up. I saw Milan Bjelica drive a vehicle belonging to an Ilijas company, drive to the Hyper Market led by Momir Andric. Then they went on to banks and other businesses. Wherever the person in charge was a Serb --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat these names, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat the names that you just mentioned for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So for all their support, they needed the finance, the alcohol, the food, it was Mirko Ostojic, the professor of mathematics in Ilijas who was in charge. That was his job. The people who led various businesses and shops and who provided the goods were Milan Bjelica, the manager in the butcher's shop in Ilijas, and that butcher's shop belonged to Ilpit in Ilijas. Market number 10 was managed by Momir Andric. Ilpit's shop near the bank and the shop in Podlugovi, where the manager was Mirko Andric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to work during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I continued to work until the 26th of May, when I was met at the doorstep by Zdravko Djuric, who served me with a decision that I have to turn over my shop to a Serb, Miroslav Delipara. This order was certified by the stamp of the Serbian Democratic Party, and the signature was that of Trifko Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would like to call up 65 ter number 4272. No, sorry, that's incorrect. It should be 65 ter number 7229.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1055, we have a document now on the screen. Could you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking at that decision that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Djuric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Djuric was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you had to hand over the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got to mention that all the members of the Serbian [as interpreted] and Croatian ethnic communities, in the health centre, in the ironworks, or in the education system, were replaced because they were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my turn came to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. It's not the Serbian and Croatian ethnic communities, but Muslim and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were replaced by ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you -- where did you stay after the 26th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beginning with the 26th of May, I was at my home in Ljesevo. In that period, I tried to get my family out on the regional road, Ilijas-Visoko. However, at the roadblock at the present border of the Sarajevo-Zenica canton, near the tavern called Izlet there was a roadblock manned by policemen from the police station of Ilijas. They did not let me through. One of them was an active-duty policeman, and I knew him privately. His name was Stanisic. And another young man was with him. They turned me back. This young man, named Cedo, was wearing a uniform of the reserve police. I went back home with my family across the hill. I took my family away to Vrbovik, and I remained to run some errands and finish some business, because I had some small cattle and one cow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court, why did you try to send your family away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We still had electricity. The television and radio reported daily on crimes being committed in the areas Bijeljina, Zvornik, Brcko. It was clear that those things were coming closer to us, and of course I was looking for safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us, what did you hear about what was happening in those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, every day news came of crimes committed. Television broadcasts showed dead bodies in the streets of Zvornik. It was quite clear that one should run away. The radio reported -- I remember one specific thing, that Arkan's and Seselj's units entered Bijeljina and freed the town from Muslims, as they put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What station did you get this information from, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The radio and television I had were tuned mostly to Radio and TV Sarajevo, and the reporters reported from the various towns concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what the situation was like in your village between the day that you sent your family away and the 4th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the time my family left across the hill to Breza municipality, things seemed to be pretty calm. You didn't see much people around. Many had left already. You could say it was calm until that fatal day, the 4th of June, around 1700 hours. There was just one shot heard, which was a sign -- a signal to start firing at our village from all sorts of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when this shot was fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my home some 300, 400 metres away. I had a brother who lived there. I started walking there, and on the way a lady neighbour, Salema Fazlic, asked me to have coffee with her. We talked behind a house nearby, drinking coffee, when the firing started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe the nature of the fire that you talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All across the village, shells started falling. You could hear infantry weapons firing, fire from all types of weapons. In the village, there were no armed units to put up any resistance. Instead, we managed to run to the basement of that woman. At first, there were five or six of us, and then other neighbours from nearby houses ran to join us, trying to find some safety in that basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned infantry weapons and fire from all sort of weapons. Was there artillery fire as well, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were with you in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With me in the basement, there were Suad Masnopita, Senahid Fazlic, Salema Fazlic, Amir Fazlic, Mahmut Fazlic, later we were joined by Osman Omanovic, Bulbul, Hasan, Bulbul, Munib, so every moment the number of us in the basement increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the fire -- the weapons fire last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The firing lasted until 3.00 p.m., which was not quite enough for us to run away. We reckoned there would be no more firing, but instead it continued, and it didn't stop this time until we were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see, from the basement, what happened to any of the houses around where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point, Amir Fazlic looked through the blinds, which were down. He peered through the blinds and he saw Munib Bulbul's house burning some ten metres away from us. At that time, we decided to try running away. Amir was the first to go, then Muharem Islamovic, Dzevad Salkic. I was supposed to be the fourth to go. However, when my turn came, Amir and Salkic came back wounded, and I realised that it would be a futile attempt. At that moment, the attackers came close to us, making a lot of noise and racket, shooting, calling to us to come out. We came out with our arms raised. They pushed us to the ground, asking for money, passports. They took all the jewellery off the women, earrings, bracelets, rings, whatever they had. And then they told us to stand up, intending to put us back in the basement. And then Vasilije Vidovic approached, accompanied by a blonde young man. At that moment, Amir, wounded, fell to the ground. He was shot in the head, and that made me suspect that Vasilije Vidovic was the killer, or perhaps the blonde young man who was with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a brief moment. Where were you standing when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was standing outside, and Amir, wounded, had been standing next to me outside the house, on a concrete slab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was standing next to you outside the house when he was shot and fell to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see who fired the shot that killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only people coming towards us were Vasilije and this blonde young man. It could be only one of the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, we were put in the basement again. They obviously intended to kill us, because they were saying, "Get in, get in." They pushed us into the basement, fell us to the ground. Some of them used the occasion to stand on our backs and take photos of themselves. However, then came an order, "Get them out." We walked out, we formed a file, and they took us to Ilijas. At the head of the file --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, we'll get back to this in just one moment. But you said you were being pushed back into the basement because you were going to get killed. Why did you think at the time that you would be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we heard voices saying, "Kill them, burn the place down."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm kindly reminded, and I'm afraid I'll forget if I don't, now ask for an exhibit number for 65 ter number 7229. That is the document that the witness was given on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Please allow me to come back to this document. I have a series of questions to put on it, and we cannot admit the document before putting these questions. On the 27th of May, 1992, three people, a commission, comes to assess the stock or the property or valuables you have in your home at 8.00 in the morning. Did three people come to your house at 8.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two persons. One was missing and we had to wait for him. It was Jovica Radic who had not come. Zdravko replaced him with Kasim Rozijic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore they looked around to see what kind of goods you had in your house, food stuffs and things, and the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was working in the trade of electrical supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they counted and numbered the cables, the electric wires, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a register of debits and credits, things taken out, sold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seemingly, according to this document, Miroslav Delipara, who was in charge of this, he had to take charge of all this equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He took over the whole shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. There is the equipment, on the one hand, and goods. On listening to the Prosecutor and you, one has the feeling that there is a transfer of goods of the entire assets. And on reading this document, as a legal expert, I understand that it is the equipment that relate to a decision taken on the 25th, 26th, 27th, which we don't have, was set aside. You were told to leave the house; it no longer belongs to you, it now belongs to Miroslav Delipara, or were you told that the equipment will be entrusted to Miroslav Delipara? This is not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Delipara became the manager of the shop, and I, as the previous manager, turn over the whole inventory and the goods that were in the shop at that moment. I was replaced as manager because I was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Let me finish. You have just talked about a manager. You were the manager? When you manage, you manage on behalf of someone. You're not the owner in that case. Who did this shop belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Velepromet Company, Visoko, under the umbrella of Trgopromet, Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were the manager not the owner, therefore, they just changed managers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was a change of managers; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was a replacement of the manager. I was removed from my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the risk of having time deducted, I have to draw your attention to one thing. You have a list of the commission who handled the turnover. Two members of the commission are Muslims, and one Serb woman was with them. Maybe it's not easy for you to assess it yourselves, but since you asked the question, I thought it would be of assistance. Now it's on your conscience whether you would deduct it from my time. So it can't have been the reason, just that he was a Muslim. There must have been another reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's a change of managers. That's what we are told. A Serb is on the commission; what do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see on the decision that number 2 was a Serb who had not come. He hadn't showed up. You see, Rajko Djuric's signature. He put Kasim Rozajic in the place of the missing one. The third men was Mensura Hadzic [phoen], who got the same decision I did, replacing her from her job, just because we were both Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the number 2 on the original document in your language, we can see that the name has been crossed out and replaced by "Kasim," I can't read it very well, there's a name here. And he is a Muslim, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kasim Rozajic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a Muslim, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was an assistant in the shop next-door. He lost his job the very next day because he was a Muslim. So all Muslims, not Kasim, Mensura and I alone, but everybody, all the Muslims. Osman Vrcok [phoen] was replaced by Rade Skando [phoen]. Let me not enumerate all the Muslims who were replaced. The whole business was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Mr. Seselj will address this during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to put to the witness. This commission was in charge of assessing the inventory and the equipment, or could the commission have people replaced? Did it have the authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision to replace the people was made by the Crisis Staff of Ilijas, signed by Trifko Radic, the SDS, and these people came to count the goods there. The financial situation, the assets, what was missing, what was there. So that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the financial situation was good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this document -- this document has to do with the inventory, not to do with the change of managers. And you are telling us that as a result of this, a manager was changed, so it's now on the record. This document only aims at drawing up the inventory; do you agree with me here or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not agree, because you see what it says in that decision? It says: "Decision on bookkeeping and establishing what (redacted) on appointing the commission for the inventory of commodities and other material goods in the shop (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P456, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Maybe out of an abundance of caution we should redact, at page 52, line 7, the precise reference to the depot that is in question, just to avoid identifying the witness with such precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Mr. Marcussen hasn't continued the examination-in-chief yet, so since there's a lull and a pause, could you instruct him that during the next break, he provide me with the transcripts of the testimony of this witness in the other trial that we mentioned at the beginning? I don't want to mention the trial's name, so that we don't have to go into private session, but the Prosecution must disclose that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, in case you do have the witness's testimony during the trial which was mentioned earlier today, please disclose it to him. You are nodding to the contrary, so this means you don't have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, we don't have the transcript of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that can be done in 15 minutes by fax, and the Prosecution must provide that. And the Prosecution, I am sure, cooperates very well with that court and we can have it here in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, just a minute, please. I was in your job for decades, and I know that technically speaking, you can send an immediate request to your colleague to ask him to be provided with a copy of the testimony. Technically speaking, this is perfectly feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, two -- a few points on this. First of all, the Prosecution only learned that the witness had testified before the State Court yesterday, so we wouldn't have had time to obtain the transcript. The accused is assisted by -- I think we're now up to 36 people that is on his Defence team. He certainly had the resources to request any kind of information that he wished to receive. We now have the problem that the witness testified with protective measures before the State Court, and it might actually therefore not be quite so easy to obtain this material from the State Court. So there's no way that we can provide the accused with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I agree with you, but in this trial you're not the only person present. There's Mr. Mundis and Mrs. Dahl and other people. One of your colleagues can make a phone call and call up the Prosecutor in charge and say, "We have heard that. Can you check this with the Registry of the State Court and see whether this can be provided to us either in English or in B/C/S, whether we can have the testimony." The person at the other end of the line will say either, "Yes," or, "No, I can't because I've nobody to do this and I'm alone. This can be done in two minutes." I'm not going to phone up. Why not? I can, and I can ask the Prosecutor to have this testimony. I can demand it of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we're on the subject, I'd like to say that if the Trial Chamber requests this from the Prosecution, I understand, but I don't agree with the fact that the accused can say, as he did on line 18 -- page 18, I'm sorry, line 23, that the accused must provide this. It is for the Prosecution to conduct its own investigations, and the Prosecution does its job as it deems fit, hopefully. And it's only the Trial Chamber that can order this; it's not the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, after my colleague's statement, does this not come under your obligations, Mr. Mundis; i.e., that you are under the obligation to disclose this under Rule 66 and 68, anything which you may have and which you must disclose to the accused? The testimony might be exculpatory. Then it would be under Rule 68. If it's not exculpatory, then it would come under Rule 66. This is a question I have for you, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's a very short answer to that, Mr. President, and that is if it's in our possession. This material is not in our possession. Therefore, there is no obligation for us to disclose it, because we cannot disclose that which we do not have. Similarly, there is no obligation for us to go out and get this material. If the accused wants it, as Mr. Marcussen has said, he can go and get it. Now, the next problem is a -- or problems would be a series of practical and legal issues that are intertwined. I know, from dealings with the State Court in the past, that if a witness testifies with protective measures, that material will not be given to us in the absence of a court order. That, of course, has to be done by the Chamber of the State Court, which can be done and can be arranged if this Trial Chamber were to issue an order directing them or asking them to do so. I will also make it clear to the Chamber that the State Court does not maintain transcripts. What they can provide us with are recordings of proceedings. There are summary records made, but there is no verbatim transcript made of proceedings before the State Court. So the best we could hope for would be getting tapes that would require orders of this Trial Chamber and an order of the State Court Trial Chamber to make those tapes available. I would expect we could have such tapes or such material in probably two or three weeks, but we certainly are not going to be able to get something faxed to us, nor are we most likely going to be even in a position where I could get audio files e-mailed to me from the State Court. There are practical and logistical considerations involved. As I indicated, this will require orders of this Trial Chamber and of the Trial Chamber of the State Court. But I want to be absolutely clear that our obligation extends to material that's in our possession. We don't possess this. Therefore, there's nothing for us to disclose with respect to this witness's testimony to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have heard what the position of the Prosecution is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, according to an appeals judgement in Delalic et al, the Appeals Chamber gave a definition which is then repeated in a whole series of judgements to the effect that the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal is an employee of international justice and he has two equally-important tasks; to prosecute suspects and to discover potentially exculpatory material to be disclosed to the accused. Those are two equally-important duties on the part of the OTP of the Tribunal. In this case, it is a witness who's already testified, and I've been provided with all the transcripts before the Special Court in Belgrade for every witness appearing here. The State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a court which has an international character of sorts because there are judges from Bosnia-Herzegovina trying there, and each time the Trial Chamber includes one international judge, so the State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sort of branch office, of sorts, of Hague Tribunal, so a court which is far closer, in organisational terms, to The Hague Tribunal than any other court in the world. And so the Prosecution must provide me with those transcripts. So I'm not asking for something that the Prosecution need not do, but I emphasise it must comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There is absolutely no obligation for the Prosecution at this institution to go out and search for exculpatory material. Certainly, under the ICC regime, that is the case. If we come across material and we have material that we identify, we disclose it. We do not go out looking for exculpatory or Rule 68 material, number 1. Number 2, I have indicated we don't have this. Even if I wanted to get it, it's doubtful that I could because of the protective measures that are involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will hand down a decision on this matter. We have heard Mr. Seselj's request. We have heard the comments on the part of the OTP, and we shall hand down a decision. We have five minutes left before the break, Mr. Marcussen. The Registrar has just told me that it is now time to have a break. We shall have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of points. We have resumed our hearing. You have approximately one hour left, Mr. Marcussen. Normally speaking, you should be able to finish if there are no procedural incidents. The second point. Mr. Seselj, one point I'd like to clarify as regards seven days. If you were to certify to appeal the decision, the deadline has been shortened to today. So if you file certification to apply, your deadline is today. Second point. The question you have put to the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber has weighed this in light of the Rules. The Prosecution need only disclose those documents that it has, but you can ask the Trial Chamber to have this document disclosed to you. So you need to file a request -- file a motion, and then the Trial Chamber will be seized of the matter. We shall now resume the examination-in-chief. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-1055, I'd like to take you back to when you were in the basement. You have explained you were in the basement and you thought you were going to be killed, and then an order came in that you should be taken out of the basement. Was anything said at the time about why you should be taken out or at whose request you were being taken out of the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard a voice telling us to come out of the basement, but I did not notice -- or, rather, I didn't hear who issued the order for us to come out of the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the order just saying you should come out of the basement or were any reasons given why you should come out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that we should come outside. And when we went outside, they ordered us to form a column and said that we would be transported to some other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe to us where the column went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As they ordered us to put something over our heads, a T-shirt, a jumper, or a jacket, or anything, the column set out in the direction of Ilijas. And on part of the road, which we call Polje, another order came to the head of the group, Boro Margetic, that the group should be turned around and directed towards Visoko. So we turned towards Visoko, and on a section of the road an APC came by, and out of it climbed Zoran Rasevic with the intention of killing us. And the leader of the group there opposed this, he prevented him from doing that, and said that Vasilije had said that he needed men for some other things. So we continued on our journey, and we reached a house, Munib Dervisevic's house, where we came across Vasilije Vidovic again, and he was shooting --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He shot in the direction of Sidic Nimza's [phoen] house, and he hit the house. We arrived at the railway station by that time, where we came across a large number of Muslims and Croats who had been captured and were grouped there at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me just ask you two questions about Vasilije Vidovic. You said he shot at a house. What did he shoot with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was shooting from his shoulder, so it must have been a Zolja-type weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a Zolja-type weapon, could you explain to us what kind of a weapon that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert in weapons, I used to be a cook in the army, but he shot from his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a rifle, is it a rocket, is it -- what kind of a weapon is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A grenade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, a Zolja is a hand-held rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- did you see how Vasilije Vidovic was transported at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vasilije went 'round in a dark blue Golf car with a flag on it. It was a black flag with the symbols that I showed you earlier on, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything in particular in his car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the back seat of his car, there was a television set which he managed to steal somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were -- when you came to the railway station, were you put in the railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this facility belonged to the railway station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and the other people in the column, were you put in the railway station or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were at the railway station in Ljesevo, and half an hour later two buses turned up. They boarded us onto the buses and drove us off towards Ilijas. They stopped at the railway station of Podlug, where they tried to put us into the basement of that station. However, that basement was already full, because the Muslims and Croats had been brought there from Ilijas. And they detained us in the old elementary school building, which at that time was used as a -- was being used as a warehouse by the company Iskra from Kranj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe how the room that you were put in looked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The room? Well, we know what a school looks like. It had six classrooms. However, because it was being used as a warehouse, they had bashed through the walls so that the vehicles moving the goods could move along that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were the first people to enter the premises from Ljesevo, but two or three days later, from the basement at the railway station that I mentioned earlier on at Podlugovi, we were -- people were transferred from there who had been incarcerated, and they had been poisoned, because through a little window some sort of bomb or -- smoke bomb had been thrown in. And from the Ilijas community of Bioca, two more buses were brought in with about 100 people, so that the number in the camp by this time had increased to between 130 and 140.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything in the room to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just wooden floors, bare wooden floors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of toilet facilities were there, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building had no water. There was just one toilet, but there was no water in the toilet either. There were five or six women with us at the time and two children. For the first seven days, we were given nothing to eat, and then after that they would give us half a loaf of bread per person for a period of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were guarding the people detained at Iskra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were locals, local Serbs who behaved -- well, I have to say this, that they behaved in a proper manner. They were elderly people. The commander was Slavko Risto [as interpreted], and the others were: Veljko Vidovic; Okrilj, Bosko; Simic; Nedzo Milic; Ljubisa Radic. Those are the ones that I can remember at present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any local people around Iskra try to help you in any way while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some people, depending perhaps on their ability, would throw in a loaf of bread, a pack of cigarettes, and there were moments as well when they would get through to us some beet, normally used for fodder, that we ate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained at Iskra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were detained in Iskra some three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point in time, did you see Vaske?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else come to Iskra that you particularly remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of times, some strangers came in, people we didn't know at least. I remember one particular moment when, in a Fiat 128, of white colour, driven with Vasilije Stolac, two men came from the position where I was looking from. One was a tall man, dark-haired, with a beard and a fur hat, and the other one did not have a beard, a stocky man, no fur hat. And I could see them talking outside. I couldn't see them while they were talking. It was like I had a sound, but no image. They were talking outside the open window about some political developments, of course, from their point of view. They told the commander of the guards to prepare ten men, that they would come to fetch them at 5.00. And one young man was taken away by them immediately. That young man was Bakir Sehic. He was later exhumed after the Dayton Accords in a hilly area overlooking Ljubos, a local community near Ilijas. We found out this young man's name was Mica. Mica entered the camp for a while, and there were some infirm elderly men and people lying down on the ground. He told them, "Get up when an officer of the Seselj's guards comes in."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were ten men taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was prevented by Slobodan Subotic, an inspector on the police force at the police station at Ilijas. He toured the camp frequently, trying to find a way to organise an exchange, because in the territory of Breza he had some family and his parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had been in Iskra, were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime in mid-August, one civilian came to the camp, accompanied by Nebojsa Spiric, who was in uniform. He informed us that buses would come and that we would be transferred somewhere in Vogosca. The buses did arrive, and we were transferred to the Svrake camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed there for another two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 65 ter number 4272. And as we prepare the exhibit, if we could zoom in, before it's being shown to the witness, just on the picture but without the text that I suspect is underneath the picture. And I venture again to suggest that this picture is number 2 in the witness binder. I hope I'm right this time. I think this is fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-1055, is this -- do you recognise the building on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a building known as Planja house, where we were kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were detained in Planja's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 20 people from Vogosca were already there in this house when we arrived. That means that together with our group, we were around 120 men, because in the meantime, in Ilijas, some exchanges of elderly people had taken place and the women who had been detained were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the conditions in Planja house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Compared to Podlugovi, a water tank came to this house. We got one meal a day, usually around 2.00 or 3.00 p.m. for those who remained in the building. However, many people were not there, because early in the morning they were taken outside to do various types of labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before we move away from the topic of the house, I would ask for an exhibit number for 65 ter number 4272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 457.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a short question. I see the house with three levels, three floors. 120 people in there, and in the morning some people work outside. But during the night, how many people were guarding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I answer this question, I must say that you can't see the basement that was underneath the whole area of the house. The house had security arrangements, locked gates and everything, and systems, so that there were only two or three men in the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were 120 of you, and two to three people guarded you; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards were members of the army, of the so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Predrag Simic, Momir Damjanovic, one named Balorda, and I can't remember his name, Simica Djuric, Stanko Knezevic, and the commander of this camp was Brano Laca [phoen]. His deputy was Nebojsa Spiric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know they were members of the VRS or the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they changed. Some went to combat duty and then came back after a while, and then their replacements would go on combat duty. And you could also tell by the weapons they had and their uniforms. You could tell they were army men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described -- you mentioned that people were being taken out to do work. What kind of work were the detainees to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People would be taken away sometime around 7.00 a.m. by a bus or a van. Brano Laco [phoen] would throw everyone outside, and then they would pick out the number they needed for a certain place. The system was, "You, you and you, get in." Men would go out to dig trenches, communicating trenches, to chop wood, to bury the dead, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these tasks performed, and in particular where were the trenches dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The trenches were dug primarily in localities facing Zuc hill, Orlic, Sedras, Kremes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, let's save time. When you told us what had happened, the fact that you were brought together at the station and then loaded on buses and so on, as I was listening to you I was saying to myself, "Such an operation could not have been put together by just a few persons." It is obviously a military operation. And now you're telling us that you were guarded by the VRS and that some of the detainees were sent off to dig trenches. Very well. You were a victim, you were captured, you were made prisoner, and I'm sure that you can answer my question. According to you, the people who detained you, did they belong to the VRS or were they rogue people operating individually or as a group? What do you feel about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was definitely the army of the RS, Republika Srpska, that organised this camp. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You answered my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be sure that we understand the answer: Do you know who had organised the first place you were detained at Iskra?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know who organised that. I only know who brought me there and who arrested me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer, that the camp was organised by the VRS, that relates to Planja's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have no information about the Podlugovi camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, yourself, did you carry out any kind of labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What tasks did you perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A number of times, I dug at Sedras, Kremes, Mijatovica elevation, but later I stayed on the premises and dug graves for the dead, because every day there were deaths in the area of Zuc, where the VRS was trying to get control of that area and enter Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the places you were digging trenches, were they close to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any incidents where detainees from Planja's house were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. More than once, the VRS organised attacks on the hills I mentioned, Zuc and Orlic, and our men were used as human shields. Many got killed while being used as human shields and while performing labour for the VRS that they were forced to do. If you have no objection, I would like to enumerate a couple of those who got killed, although there were many more. Rasim Avdukic, Hasan Fazlic, Mehmet Sehic, Nermin Skando [phoen], Ramo Hadzic, Nusret Salimovic, Safet Krijeze [phoen], Najl, Durmo, Mujo Sehic, and so on and so forth. There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, participating at any instances and being used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fortunately, I was not used, myself, as a human shield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you know about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who survived, who were used as human shields, would come back to the camp and bring back the dead, those people who got killed and whom I buried myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the frontline, did you see Vaske at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On a hill overlooking Vogosca. It was during a break. Vaske showed up with his men, coming back from the frontline. He saw us, and he just said, "Are you still here?" And he went on his way. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand he meant by that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you ask me, I thought he was surprised that we were still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Planja's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime around the 22nd, 23rd October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was reunited with my family in the municipality of Visoko, a settlement of Podvinci, Gorusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these events, have you seen Vaske again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vaske Vidovic, the next time I saw him was on television, in a broadcast of Republika Srpska, during the unrest in Belgrade when a mass of people -- a throng was trying to settle scores with Mr. Vojislav Seselj, and newly -- cleanly shaven, very neat, Vasilije Vidovic stood up in his protection, got out his gun and raised it high in the air, intending to shoot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your impression that Vaske was there to protect Mr. Seselj or are you not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your impression that Vasilije Vidovic was there to somehow protect Mr. Seselj or was it just a coincidence that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the only impression you could get was he was a regular escort and bodyguard of Mr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- do you know whether Mr. Seselj visited your municipality at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll make a mistake. It was wartime. Whether it was 1993 or 1994 -- where I was living, you could catch the signal of Radio Ilijas, and the author of the programme said that Mr. Vojislav Seselj was visiting Ilijas and held a rally, made a speech in a rally with citizens. This reporter was Gordana Krunic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that report mention whether Vasilije Vidovic was also there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, in your municipality were there any destruction of religious property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we came back to the territory of our own municipality, there was not a single religious site left standing properly. They'd all been razed to the ground. And in talking to the Serbs who had remained and stayed on living there with us, I learned that this was done by Vasilije Vidovic, together with Boro Margetic, Ranko Draskic, and a man called Vitomir Lazic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this completes the direct examination of this witness by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two additional questions to put to you, Witness, please. The first one deals with Vaske. Do you know what happened to this person or did he disappear completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from what I saw on television, I don't know what happened to him, to Vasilije Vidovic, after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question: When you were in the locality, did the Muslims set up a crisis staff of their own in order to deal with what the Serbs were doing to try to control the municipality? So I would like to know whether the Muslims got together at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time in Ilijas, there were no conditions for any rallying or anything like that, or forming a crisis staff, or anything like that. The authorities had already taken control of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yourself, did you ever stand guard in your locality with a rifle or some kind of weapon that would have been given to you by the Muslim policemen in Ilijas before the locality was taken over by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stood guard only in front of our own house, with the weapons we had, our own weapons, and they were the pistols that I described. Specifically, the one I had, I had a permit issued by the police, the regular police, until all the trouble started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you were arrested, what happened to the gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pistol stayed in the house where they captured us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They found the gun or did they not find the gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what happened to the pistol. We had no further information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. A very simple one and straightforward. You told us that later on you met with Vaske, who told you, "Oh, you're still there." When you saw him, could you tell me what he was wearing? If you remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had the standard type of uniform. He used it in the attack on Ljesevo, and he was wearing that same uniform up there, which means that Vaske had the sajkaca type of cap, he had glasses, and he imitated Draza Mihajlovic. Although he could see perfectly well without the glasses. He didn't actually need to wear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is Draza Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Draza Mihajlovic, through history, the history that I was taught at school, and if that history was correct, he was a war criminal who was condemned and sentenced to death and executed, and from the Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one question to you, Mr. Witness. You told us that when Vasilije Vidovic came back from his war experience in Knin, he was escorted -- or he came with a group of approximately 20 persons who, over time, turned Chetnik. My question is: Did you ever see any of these gentlemen later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't turn Chetnik, they arrived as Chetniks. They were Chetniks already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks for this clarification, but my question was: Did you run into them at any later point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't. They were foreigners. They weren't from our parts at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So they did not stay in the Ilijas area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war, they most probably were there. But after the war, they left, and we had no further contacts with that group afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me be more precise. Did you encounter any of these gentlemen during your detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We met just one group when they were coming back. I mentioned that a few minutes ago, when they were coming back from the front, and when Vasilije said, "Are you still here?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the group of Chetniks that you recognised coming from Knin, upon Mr. Vasilije Vidovic's return, were not involved, as I understand, in the detention of the captives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The group -- you said "Vasiljevic." Did you mean "Vidovic"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, "Vidovic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vidovic's group was there, and it attacked all the villages in the Ilijas area. They had come there precisely to do that, to attack the villages. They came as warriors, as fighters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that they were taking part in the conflict. My question was if they were also involved in the detention of the people with whom you were detained. Did you ever see them in either the Iskra facility or later on in Planja's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the arrest, after they arrested people from the village and attacked the village, those people were incarcerated and they no longer appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have until a quarter past 1.00. Mr. Seselj, you can start your cross-examination, which will be continued tomorrow. Just a minute. Mr. Marcussen is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: One request of the accused. The accused has notified the Prosecution that he will use documents from Defence exhibit binder number 1 from when the Reynaud Theunens testified. The binder has 63 documents in it. We have not been notified of which documents the accused intends to use, so we would request that the accused maybe, before he uses any of the documents tomorrow, would advise us which documents he intends to use. Thank you, that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I will be using all of them. Perhaps I won't use a single one, just like the Prosecution did yesterday, precisely the same way, when you infiltrated those documents related to Nikola Poplasen, whereas they had nothing to do with the witness that was testifying. So that's precisely what I'm going to do. I'm going to give you measure for measure. May I start my cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement arrived just an hour ago. Could it please be photocopied, because I'm going to use it today. It's just two pages' long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was the statement made by?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By General Dragan Josipovic, the famous general of the Army of Republika Srpska. He was the deputy chief of the General Staff at one time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is this a document we have been notified of? Is it in binder 1, and if so, under what tab? If it has not -- if it's not in binder 1, then we have not been notified of the use of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I believe that this document was faxed to him. Therefore, it is not in the binder. This is a document which was faxed to him a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then I would request that we be given a copy of the document and that the accused only use the document during cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I provided the document to be copied, but I'm going to use it today during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, can't you use this document tomorrow, because the Prosecution would like to have time to run through it, even though this is a request made by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
